entities.name: Chan Chan
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Chan Chan, the largest mud-brick city in pre-Columbian America, thrived in the Moche Valley of northern Peru around 850 CE. This remarkable archaeological site, spanning approximately 20 square kilometers, is considered the capital of the Chimú Kingdom, which flourished until its conquest by the Inca Empire in the late 15th century. Chan Chan's unique architectural features, including its intricately decorated walls and vast urban planning, underscore its significance as a center of political and economic power during the Medieval period in South America.

The city was not merely a residential hub; it served as a major center for the production and trade of textiles and metalwork, showcasing the advanced skills of its inhabitants. The Chimú people, who constructed Chan Chan, utilized innovative irrigation techniques to support agriculture in the arid coastal environment, leading to increased agricultural output. Key structures such as the Tschudi Palace exemplify the advanced engineering and artistic achievements of the Chimú, which included elaborate friezes of fish, birds, and geometric designs, reflecting their cultural and spiritual beliefs.

Chan Chan's decline began in the late 15th century as the Inca Empire expanded, ultimately leading to its conquest around 1470 CE. However, the legacy of Chan Chan persists in the cultural memory of the Andean people, influencing subsequent Andean civilizations, including the Incas, who adopted and adapted many Chimú practices. The remnants of Chan Chan continue to serve as a vital source of archaeological and anthropological insights, shedding light on pre-Columbian urban planning and societal organization in South America.
